03.actor: A man from Eretz Yisrael who owed a levirate marriage to a woman in Babylonia
03.event: He asked Rabbi Hanina whether he could travel to Babylonia to marry his late brother's widow.
03.turn: Rabbi Hanina answered with scorn, blessing God for killing the brother who had left the Land to marry a foreign woman.
03.outcome: Rabbi Hanina's rebuke implies the man should not follow his brother out of Eretz Yisrael.
03.summary: A man whose brother had died left a widow living far away in Babylonia. He came to Rabbi Hanina and asked if he could go down there to marry her. Rabbi Hanina answered that the brother had married a foreign woman outside the Land and died, and he thanked God for it. He asked whether this man now meant to follow him down, which signals that he should stay.

04.actor: A son-in-law who passed his father-in-law's house, and Rav Sheshet
04.event: Rav Sheshet flogged a man who merely walked past his father-in-law's doorway.
04.turn: The ruling seemed to contradict the rule that only a resident son-in-law is flogged, and was explained by rumors about the man and his mother-in-law.
04.outcome: The flogging was justified by the suspicion of intimacy with his mother-in-law.
04.summary: A son-in-law walked past the entrance of his father-in-law's house and Rav Sheshet had him flogged. This seemed odd, since Rav flogged only a son-in-law who lived there. The explanation is that there were rumors about him and his mother-in-law, and passing by fed them.
04.missing: Only a brief report embedded in a legal discussion of when Rav flogged; no scene or detail of the incident itself.

05.event: Rav Hamnuna challenged Rava with a baraita and Rava had no answer.
05.turn: After Hamnuna left, Rava thought of Rabbi Elazar's opinion as an answer, doubted it, then confirmed it with another baraita.
05.outcome: Rava concluded the challenge could be dismissed as Rabbi Elazar's view alone.
05.summary: Rav Hamnuna posed a difficulty from a baraita and Rava stayed silent. Once Hamnuna had left, Rava scolded himself for not answering that it follows Rabbi Elazar. He then worried the answer might fail, but found a baraita showing Rabbi Elazar did rule that way in this case, so the challenge fell.
05.missing: It is mostly Rava's internal legal reasoning; the only events are the silence and the afterthoughts.

06.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi on his deathbed
06.event: He summoned each of his sons in turn to transmit instructions before dying.
06.turn: He called for his younger son Shimon, then his older son Gamliel, giving each the role he needed.
06.outcome: Shimon received the orders of wisdom and Gamliel the procedures of the Nasi plus a charge to rule assertively; the death itself is not shown.
06.summary: As Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi neared death, he asked for his younger son. Shimon came and was taught the orders of wisdom. Then he asked for his older son, Rabban Gamliel, passed on the procedures of the Nasi, and told him to lead assertively and cast fear on his students.
06.missing: The beginning and the end of the deathbed narrative lie outside the passage; the segments show only two transmissions.

07.event: Ravina, visiting Mehoza, told his host to take the slaughter knife to Rava for inspection.
07.turn: The host objected that Rava teaches a scholar may check his own knife, since he is the one slaughtering.
07.outcome: Ravina replied that since he was only buying the meat, Rava's principle did not apply, so the knife needed to be shown to Rava.
07.summary: Ravina arrived in Mehoza and his host showed him a slaughter knife. Ravina told him to take it to Rava, the local sage. The host protested that Rava allows a scholar to check his own knife, but Ravina answered that he was only buying the meat, so that did not apply.

08.actor: A man who made a conditional bill of divorce
08.event: He said his bill of divorce would take effect if he did not marry by the New Moon of Adar, then claimed on that date he had meant Nisan.
08.turn: His disavowal raised the question whether his claim could cancel the condition.
08.outcome: No outcome in the story; the Gemara only notes the matter turns on a dispute of Abaye and Rava.
08.summary: A man told witnesses that if he did not marry his betrothed by the New Moon of Adar, his document would be a bill of divorce. When the date arrived he said he had actually said Nisan. The Gemara asks what to be concerned about and says it is an Abaye-Rava dispute.
08.missing: No resolution of the case itself is given; it is a legal case summary.

09.event: Rabbi Hanina regularly sent four dinars to a poor man, and one Shabbat eve his wife brought it back saying he did not need it.
09.turn: She had overheard people asking the man whether he dined off silver or gold tablecloths, suggesting he was not truly poor.
09.outcome: Rabbi Hanina said they should thank swindlers, since without them we would sin every day.
09.summary: Rabbi Hanina used to send a poor man four dinars every Friday. One day his wife came back and said the man did not need it, because she heard people asking whether he ate off silver or gold tablecloths. Rabbi Hanina answered that this is why we should be grateful to swindlers, since otherwise we would be guilty of neglecting the poor every day.

10.actor: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak, who danced before brides, and Rabbi Zeira
10.event: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak danced at weddings juggling three myrtle branches, and Rabbi Zeira complained that the old man was humiliating the scholars.
10.turn: When he died a pillar of fire separated him from everyone else, a sign granted to only one or two per generation.
10.outcome: Rabbi Zeira then said the old man's branch, or nonsense, or method had worked for him.
10.summary: Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai used to dance before brides with a myrtle branch, and Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak juggled three branches, prompting Rabbi Zeira to complain the old man was embarrassing the scholars. When Rav Shmuel died, a pillar of fire parted him from everyone, a rare honor. Rabbi Zeira then conceded that his branch, his foolishness or his method had worked in his favor.

11.event: He performed halitza with a slipper, alone, and at night.
11.turn: Shmuel sarcastically remarked on how powerful he must be to follow an individual opinion.
11.outcome: No outcome; the Gemara goes on to explain what bothered Shmuel.
11.summary: Rabba bar Hiyya performed a halitza ceremony using a non-leather slipper, as the only judge, and at night. Shmuel commented dryly on how great a man must be to rely on an individual opinion.
11.missing: No development or resolution; it is a brief report and a remark, with the explanation given in legal discussion.

12.event: Abaye taught a halakha in Rav Yosef's name and Rav Safra challenged it with two mishnayot.
12.turn: Abaye resolved the first objection but fell silent on the second.
12.outcome: Abaye reported the challenge to Rav Yosef, who said he should have answered that members of a Paschal group are vigilant.
12.summary: Abaye was reciting a ruling of Rav Yosef when Rav Safra objected with a mishna about a scroll rolling away. Abaye answered that one, but when Rav Safra raised a second objection about lowering the Paschal lamb into the oven, he stayed silent. Later he told Rav Yosef, who asked why he had not answered that Paschal group members are vigilant.

13.event: Ulla visited Pumbedita, saw Rav Yehuda's grown son unmarried, and asked why.
13.turn: Rav Yehuda said he could not know where to find a woman of sound lineage, and Ulla said nobody can be sure of his own lineage and cited verses to show how doubtful ancestry can be.
13.outcome: Asked what to do, Ulla advised judging lineage by who falls silent first in a quarrel.
13.summary: Ulla visited Rav Yehuda and asked why his grown son was still unmarried. Rav Yehuda said he did not know where to find a suitable wife given lineage concerns. Ulla said none of them knew their own origins for certain, then, when Rav Yehuda asked what to do, told him to follow the silence: the one who is silent first in a quarrel is of better stock.
13.missing: Much of the passage is a lineage argument and verse interpretation (segments 5-7), so the story is thin.

14.actor: A man who left a will for his daughter's dowry, and Rav Idi bar Avin
14.event: A man instructed his heirs to give his daughter a dowry, and the cost of dowries then fell.
14.turn: The question arose who gets the savings.
14.outcome: Rav Idi bar Avin ruled the savings go to the orphans.
14.summary: A man told his heirs to give his daughter a dowry. Before they did, dowry prices dropped, leaving a surplus. Rav Idi bar Avin ruled the saving belongs to the sons.
14.missing: It is a bare legal case with no characters or detail beyond the ruling.

15.actor: Hama, son of Rabba bar Abbahu
15.event: Hama paid Avimi's debt to the people of Bei Hozai and asked for the document back.
15.turn: They refused, claiming the money was for a different, undocumented debt.
15.outcome: Before Rabbi Abbahu, Hama had no witnesses, and Abbahu ruled he could get neither money nor document back.
15.summary: Avimi sent money with Hama to pay a debt in Bei Hozai. Hama paid and asked for the debt document, but they said the payment covered a different debt and kept it. Rabbi Abbahu asked if Hama had witnesses, and when he had none, ruled that since they could have denied any payment at all, they could also claim it was for side debts.

18.actor: A betrothed couple and Rav Yosef
18.event: A betrothed man and his pregnant betrothed came to Rav Yosef, she saying the child was his.
18.turn: The man admitted the child was his.
18.outcome: Rav Yosef ruled there was no cause for concern, since he admitted it and the law follows Rabban Gamliel.
18.summary: A betrothed couple came before Rav Yosef because the woman was pregnant and said it was by him. The man agreed it was his. Rav Yosef said there was nothing to worry about, since he admitted it and the law follows Rabban Gamliel.
18.missing: The man's reply is split across the segment break but is present in segment 5.
